tier_reason: The README Benchmarks table (sum of 1,000 integers, averaged over 1,000 runs) lists Minarrow IntegerArray direct 88 ns and via enum 124 ns against arrow-rs Int64Array struct 147 ns and dyn 181 ns. It states the CPU (Intel Core Ultra 7 155H), the compiler (Rust 1.97-nightly) and a release build. The code is public in benches/hotloop_benchmark_avg_std.rs (N=1000, ITERATIONS=1000, harness=false, cast_arrow feature), and its header gives the run command RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo bench.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Sum of 1,000 i64, averaged over 1,000 runs: Minarrow IntegerArray direct 88 ns vs arrow-rs Int64Array (struct) 147 ns and arrow-rs Int64Array (dyn) 181 ns, about 1.7x-2.1x faster (derived from page data). Minarrow via enum dispatch is 124 ns (about 1.2x-1.5x vs arrow-rs, derived from page data), and a raw Vec<i64> is 85 ns. The Rust->Python handoff (1M rows, 2 cols) is 165 ns and Python->Rust is 2.5 us, but these are standalone figures with no Arrow/pyarrow comparison.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.97-nightly, release build (cargo bench; the repo sets no custom [profile], so default opt-level 3). The bench file header recommends RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native", but the README does not confirm it was used for the published numbers.
corrections.caveats: This is a micro-benchmark of a single primitive (a scalar sum over 1,000 elements), not a query-engine workload, and the results may not generalize. The benchmark code is benches/hotloop_benchmark_avg_std.rs; no raw output is published. Each timed region includes wrapping the pre-built Vec into the array. The arrow-rs paths sum through per-index int.value(i) calls rather than iterating the values() slice, while the Minarrow paths iterate a slice. The gap may therefore reflect the access pattern chosen for Arrow, not an inherent arrow-rs cost. Timings are nanosecond-scale Instant measurements and are noise-sensitive.

notes: Every number in the claim is on the page. The record's caveat that the benchmark code "lives in examples" was wrong: it is in benches/ (only the Python roundtrip points to the pyo3 examples), so I corrected it. The fairness caveat about arrow-rs value(i) versus slice iteration is worth keeping. The metadata (Apache-2.0, 100 stars, last commit 2026-09-21, not a fork) all checks out.

tier_reason: These are first-party numbers from public scripts (bench/bench_all.sh, bench/bench_taxi.sh, with DuckDB pinned at 1.5.5 in bench/DUCKDB_VERSION). The CPU is named only for some sections (Apple M2 Pro; the headline taxi section says only "Apple M-series"). The build flags appear only as the scripts' prerequisite (zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast), and the Zig version is only the README's "tested with 0.15.2", not tied to the runs. So methodology is partial and the tier stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Against DuckDB on the raw CSV (BENCHMARKS.md). 2M-row/56MB aggregates, GROUP BY and DISTINCT on Apple M2 Pro: 2.9x-11.3x faster (6.8x-11.3x excluding MEDIAN GROUP BY at 2.9x; e.g. COUNT(*) 0.012s vs 0.136s), with 1.8MB vs 63.5MB memory. Output formats: 5.7x-8.6x. Joins: 9x-89x. LIKE on 5M rows/173MB (Apple M2): ~19x-36x. IN-subquery on a 4-core Xeon VM: ~5x down to even at 1M resolved values. NYC Taxi, 20M rows/8GB CSV (Apple M-series; csvql 2.6.0 vs DuckDB 1.5.5): 3.1x-3.4x faster with ~6x less peak memory. Also ~1.9x vs DataFusion 52.1.0 and 2.2x-2.5x vs Polars 2.0.0-rc.1 on the 1M-row taxi sample.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: The bench scripts require building with zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast. The README says it needs Zig 0.13.0+ and was tested with 0.15.2; the benchmark page names no compiler version for the runs.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark. The ReleaseFast build appears only as a prerequisite in the bench scripts, the Zig version is not tied to the published runs, and the headline NYC Taxi section names only "Apple M-series" with no specific CPU, so it falls short of tier A. The benchmark hardware varies by section (M2 Pro, M2, M-series, and a 4-core Xeon VM that the page itself says is not comparable). The gains are workload-sensitive. MEDIAN GROUP BY is only 2.9x, and IN-subquery drops to parity at 1M resolved values after a ~20x loss was found and fixed. The small-file gaps are inflated by DuckDB process and CSV-reader startup, which the author acknowledges. Results were checked for equality against DuckDB with bench/verify_correctness.sh.

notes: The benchmark page backs every claimed number except the aggregate range, which I widened to include MEDIAN (2.9x). The record's statement that build flags are not stated was only partly true, so I corrected compiler_and_flags and the caveats. The metadata (MIT, 28 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, not a fork) checks out.

tier_reason: The README Performance Benchmark table has exactly the claimed times (DuckDB 1.3.2 at 20.54s; Parquet Sort at 18.34s on Corretto 24, 24.47s on GraalVM 24 and 16.30s on GraalVM Native), and the code is public (benchmarks.sh, graal_pgo.sh, duckdb_benchmark.py). The page names only an EC2 c7i.4xlarge instance, not a CPU model. The JVM and native-image flags appear only in the scripts, and the parquetforge dependency is built from unpinned origin/master. This is first-party with partial methodology, so the tier stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Time to read, sort and write TPC-H SF10 lineitem.parquet (59M rows) on l_shipdate: DuckDB 1.3.2 20.54s. Parquet Sort takes 18.34s on Corretto 24 (about 1.12x faster), 24.47s on GraalVM 24 JIT (slower) and 16.30s as a GraalVM Native Image (about 1.26x faster). Ratios are derived from page data.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: JVM run (benchmarks.sh): -Xms16g -Xmx16g -XX:+UseParallelGC -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch. Native image (graal_pgo.sh): PGO-instrumented build, then native-image --gc=G1 -march=native -O3 --pgo=default.iprof --no-fallback. JDKs are Corretto 24 and GraalVM 24 (exact builds not stated). DuckDB is the Python package, installed unpinned by pip.
corrections.caveats: First-party single-workload benchmark (the sort only, using bucket sort because l_shipdate has a narrow range). The page names only the EC2 c7i.4xlarge instance type, not a CPU model, and the flags live in the scripts rather than on the page, so it is capped at tier C. The margin over DuckDB is modest: about 1.26x for the PGO-optimized GraalVM Native build and about 1.12x on Corretto 24, while GraalVM 24 JIT is slower than DuckDB. Times are wall-clock via bash time, including Python/JVM startup. The DuckDB side writes through a persistent data.duckdb connection. The author labels the project a performance demo not intended for production.

notes: The numbers match the page exactly. I corrected the caveat that said no flags were stated (they are in benchmarks.sh and graal_pgo.sh). I also noted that Corretto 24 beats DuckDB too, not just the Native build. The metadata (Apache-2.0, 2 stars, last commit 2025-08-06, which makes it stale at about 13.7 months) checks out.
